_comment: The statement bank for the Pathogens And Antibiotics game (True or false blitz, 20 statements across 3 rounds). Each slot holds the same idea as a TRUE version and a FALSE version, so a student's draw can flip. Every statement was fact-checked against NHS, WHO, UKHSA and OpenStax (see the unit notes). Rounds: 1 = the whole unit's basics, 2 = the misconceptions of today's lesson, 3 = far past the lesson. 'why' is the one-line correction shown after a statement; 'mistake' names the thinking behind a wrong answer. 'conflicts' lists pairs of slots that give each other away, so a game never draws both.

slots.true: Bacteria have no nucleus.
slots.false: Bacteria keep their DNA inside a nucleus.
slots.why: A prokaryote is an organism whose cell has no nucleus. Its DNA lies in the cytoplasm.
slots.mistake: Confusing bacteria with your own cells.

slots.true: A plasmid is a small ring of extra DNA.
slots.false: A plasmid is the main DNA loop of a bacterium.
slots.why: The main DNA loop is one big loop. A plasmid is a small spare ring, separate from it.
slots.mistake: Mixing up the main loop and the plasmid.

slots.true: Most bacteria reproduce by binary fission.
slots.false: Bacteria reproduce by mating with another bacterium.
slots.why: In binary fission one cell copies its DNA and splits into two identical cells. Mating is not how bacteria reproduce.
slots.mistake: Thinking bacteria need two parents.

slots.true: With plenty of food, one bacterium that divides every 20 minutes becomes 8 bacteria in 1 hour.
slots.false: With plenty of food, one bacterium that divides every 20 minutes becomes 6 bacteria in 1 hour.
slots.why: 1 hour is 3 divisions of 20 minutes, and 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. Each division doubles the number.
slots.mistake: Adding 2 each time, or multiplying 3 by 2, instead of doubling.

slots.true: Archaea and bacteria are two different groups of prokaryote.
slots.false: Archaea are a type of bacteria.
slots.why: Archaea are a separate domain. They look like bacteria but their chemistry and DNA differ.
slots.mistake: Thinking that no nucleus means bacteria.

slots.true: Archaea live in ordinary places, such as soil and the sea, as well as extreme places.
slots.false: Archaea live only in extreme places.
slots.why: Many archaea live in soil and sea water. They are just famous for living in hot springs and salt lakes.
slots.mistake: Thinking archaea and extreme places go together.

slots.true: Cyanobacteria make their own food using light.
slots.false: Cyanobacteria feed on dead plants and animals.
slots.why: Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic. Decomposers are the ones that feed on dead things.
slots.mistake: Swapping photosynthetic and decomposer.

slots.true: A typical adult has about as many bacterial cells in their body as human cells.
slots.false: A typical adult has about ten times as many bacterial cells in their body as human cells.
slots.why: Careful counting gives about 38 trillion bacterial cells and 30 trillion human cells: roughly 1 to 1. The old 10 to 1 figure is out of date.
slots.mistake: Repeating an old textbook figure.

slots.true: Some bacteria help plants get the nitrogen they need.
slots.false: Plants can use the nitrogen gas in the air directly.
slots.why: Rhizobium bacteria in the root nodules of peas and beans turn nitrogen gas into a form the plant can use.
slots.mistake: Thinking that nitrogen in the air is usable.

slots.true: Bacteria that carry the human insulin gene can make human insulin.
slots.false: Bacteria make human insulin naturally, and scientists just collect it.
slots.why: The human gene is put into a plasmid, and the bacteria then follow its instructions.
slots.mistake: Forgetting the gene was added.

slots.true: Bread rises because of yeast, which is a fungus.
slots.false: Bread rises because of bacteria.
slots.why: Yeast is a fungus. Yoghurt and fermented pickles are made with bacteria, but bread is not.
slots.mistake: Thinking every food microbe is a bacterium.

slots.true: Methanogens are archaea that live where there is no oxygen.
slots.false: Methanogens are bacteria that need oxygen to live.
slots.why: Methanogens are archaea. They live in swamp mud, sewage and the guts of cows, where there is no oxygen.
slots.mistake: Mixing up the groups.

slots.true: Antibiotics do not work against colds.
slots.false: Antibiotics cure colds.
slots.why: Colds are caused by viruses. Antibiotics are for bacterial infections and do nothing to a virus.
slots.mistake: Thinking every infection is a bacterial one.

slots.true: You should take antibiotics exactly as the doctor says.
slots.false: It is fine to keep leftover antibiotics to take the next time you feel ill.
slots.why: Take them as directed, and never save or share them. A doctor chooses the drug and the length of the course.
slots.mistake: Treating antibiotics as something to save.

slots.true: Bacteria become resistant to antibiotics. People do not.
slots.false: Your body becomes resistant to antibiotics.
slots.why: Resistance is what a population of bacteria evolves. A person can carry resistant bacteria, but the person is not resistant.
slots.mistake: Mixing up resistance with immunity.

slots.true: A resistant bacterium was already resistant before the antibiotic arrived.
slots.false: The antibiotic makes bacteria resistant by changing them.
slots.why: A few bacteria carry a chance mutation. The antibiotic does not cause it. It selects the bacteria that already have it.
slots.mistake: Thinking the drug causes the change.

slots.true: Resistant bacteria become common because the antibiotic kills the ones that are not resistant.
slots.false: Bacteria become resistant because they learn to cope with the antibiotic.
slots.why: Nothing learns. The ones that are not resistant die, and the resistant survivors reproduce.
slots.mistake: Thinking an individual bacterium changes on purpose.

slots.true: Resistance genes can spread from one bacterium to another on plasmids.
slots.false: Resistance genes stay inside one bacterium and its offspring.
slots.why: Some plasmids pass between bacteria, even different species. DNA can move sideways, not just from parent to offspring.
slots.mistake: Forgetting that plasmids move sideways.

slots.true: Antibiotics do not work against viruses.
slots.false: Antibiotics kill bacteria and viruses.
slots.why: Viruses are not bacteria. Antibiotics target things bacteria have, such as their cell wall, which a virus does not have.
slots.mistake: Thinking germs are all the same.

slots.true: Most bacteria are harmless or helpful.
slots.false: Most bacteria are harmful to people.
slots.why: Only a small fraction of bacteria cause disease. Many recycle nutrients, fix nitrogen or live in your gut without harm.
slots.mistake: Thinking bacteria means germs.

slots.true: Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium.
slots.false: Tuberculosis is caused by a virus.
slots.why: Tuberculosis is a bacterial disease, spread through the air, and it is treated with antibiotics.
slots.mistake: Mixing up bacterial and viral diseases.

slots.true: Cholera is spread by water that has been contaminated with a bacterium.
slots.false: Cholera is spread through the air in the same way as a cold.
slots.why: Cholera is caused by a bacterium in contaminated food or water.
slots.mistake: Mixing up how diseases spread.

slots.true: Hand gel contains alcohol, not antibiotics.
slots.false: Hand gel contains antibiotics.
slots.why: Alcohol gel is not an antibiotic. An antibiotic is a medicine for a bacterial infection.
slots.mistake: Mixing up antibiotics and antiseptics.

slots.true: Antibiotic resistance is natural selection happening in a population of bacteria.
slots.false: Antibiotic resistance is a different process from natural selection.
slots.why: There is variation, a selection pressure (the drug), survival and inheritance. It is the same mechanism as in the evolution unit.
slots.mistake: Not seeing resistance as evolution.

slots.true: A single bacterium does not become resistant in its lifetime just because the drug is there. The population changes.
slots.false: A single bacterium becomes resistant during its life because the drug changes it.
slots.why: The individual does not change. The population does, because the susceptible ones die and the resistant ones reproduce.
slots.mistake: Thinking that individuals adapt.

slots.true: Bacteria can evolve faster than animals because they have many more generations in the same time.
slots.false: Bacteria evolve more slowly than animals because they are so small.
slots.why: Evolution runs on generations. A bacterium can divide in as little as 20 minutes, so there are far more generations than in any animal.
slots.mistake: Linking evolution speed to size.

slots.true: A bacterium can pass a plasmid to a bacterium of a different species.
slots.false: A plasmid can pass between bacteria of the same species, but not between different species.
slots.why: Plasmids can move between different species, which is how resistance can spread so widely.
slots.mistake: Thinking the species boundary blocks plasmids.

slots.true: If an antibiotic kills every bacterium except one resistant one, that one's offspring will be resistant.
slots.false: If an antibiotic kills every bacterium except one resistant one, the offspring will lose the resistance.
slots.why: Resistance is inherited. Binary fission makes identical copies, so the offspring are resistant too.
slots.mistake: Forgetting that the offspring are copies.

slots.true: Using an antibiotic when it is not needed makes it more likely that resistant bacteria spread.
slots.false: Using an antibiotic when it is not needed makes it less likely that resistant bacteria spread.
slots.why: Every use is a selection pressure on all the bacteria in and on you, so the resistant ones are favoured.
slots.mistake: Thinking an unneeded dose is harmless.

slots.true: A methanogen, a cell with no nucleus that lives by making methane, is an archaean.
slots.false: A cell with no nucleus that lives in a hot spring must be an archaean.
slots.why: All methanogens are archaea. A hot spring also holds cyanobacteria and other bacteria, so where a microbe lives does not decide its group.
slots.mistake: Judging a microbe by where it lives.

slots.true: A virus that infects bacteria is neither a bacterium nor an archaean.
slots.false: A virus is a very small bacterium.
slots.why: A virus is not a cell. It cannot reproduce on its own and has to use a host cell.
slots.mistake: Seeing a virus as a tiny bacterium.

slots.true: With plenty of food, after 4 hours one bacterium that divides every 20 minutes has become 4,096.
slots.false: With plenty of food, after 4 hours one bacterium that divides every 20 minutes has become 24.
slots.why: 4 hours is 12 divisions, and 2 multiplied by itself 12 times is 4,096. 24 is what you get by multiplying 2 by 12 instead of doubling 12 times.
slots.mistake: Multiplying by the number of divisions instead of doubling.

slots.true: Most bacteria never make anyone ill.
slots.false: Most bacteria are pathogens.
slots.why: About 540 species of bacteria are known to cause disease in people. That is a small fraction of all bacteria.
slots.mistake: Seeing bacteria only as germs.

slots.true: The human insulin gene is carried into the bacterium on a plasmid.
slots.false: The human insulin gene is put into the bacterium's nucleus.
slots.why: A bacterium has no nucleus. The gene goes in on a plasmid.
slots.mistake: Forgetting that a prokaryote has no nucleus.

slots.true: Natural selection needs variation that is there before the antibiotic arrives.
slots.false: Natural selection needs the antibiotic to cause the variation.
slots.why: The variation arises by chance, before the drug. The drug only decides who survives.
slots.mistake: Thinking the environment causes the variation.

slots.true: Some bacteria in your gut make vitamins, such as vitamin K.
slots.false: No bacteria in your gut make anything that your body can use.
slots.why: Gut bacteria make vitamin K and some B vitamins, and they help to break down fibre.
slots.mistake: Thinking gut bacteria only cause trouble.
